fullText:
Humans will have to compete with AI-powered virtual employees in the near future. Here are our tips for the last human holdouts

Futureproofing your career with an AI-resistant degree is a tough ask, says Charlie Ball, an expert on graduate employment for Jisc, the UK’s higher education digital, data and technology agency.

“What you’re trying to do is futureproof a 45-year career in a time of rapid technological change – and that’s really quite hard to do. What’s likely is that jobs that hinge a lot on human, face-to-face interaction are unlikely to be replaced.”

He warns however that the discussion should focus less on identifying specific vocational paths that are safe from AI, and more on how to equip young people with a suite of skills that allow them to adapt rapidly to labour market change.

But if pushed, areas of work that might offer more protection from AI than others include the following.

Research and development
Degrees in Stem subjects (science, technology, engineering and maths) have long been associated with good careers. Although AI will inevitably affect entry-level lab work, “the creativity and imaginative work will have to be done by humans,” says Ball. “The whole point of R&D is to find out new things, and AI can only really compare against stuff that it’s already got in its database.”

Engineering
We may see AI increasingly embedded in design and modelling, but human engineers will still be required to operate in physical, real-world environments that will continue to require human oversight. “Much of engineering is going to be hard to replace by AI,” Ball says. “We are likely still to need engineers to do the big stuff like civil engineering – building bridges and buildings. Those areas are likely to be OK.”

Creative arts and entertainment
“Although AI can produce creative art, people generally don’t like it very much,” is Ball’s verdict. He thinks we will get better at spotting its handiwork. “There will always be demand for human-led creativity. Everything AI currently produces is a remix of things that already exist. AI can’t create things. You’ll never get a distinctive new voice emerging. It can’t do that.”

Medicine
“We will still have doctors in 50 years’ time,” says Ball. “Their jobs will change somewhat. But people will want humans to deliver their health news, particularly the more difficult news. And no matter how good automation gets, when your kids are poorly, you will want to take them to a human GP.” AI can be helpful with diagnoses in some cases, “but it will still make mistakes. Where you will need someone to take responsibility for decisions, they will all have to be human.”

Nursing and midwifery
“AI and tech will get injected into many health roles, and on balance that’s probably quite a good thing, because at the moment we have nowhere near enough people doing these jobs,” says Ball. “But people will want humans to care for them when they are sick. People will want humans to look after them when they are old. I cannot envisage a situation where there will ever be a robot midwife.”

Education
“Nor are we going to get robot teachers,” he adds, despite the ongoing shortage of teachers in England. “There is already a role for technology in facilitating the delivery of education. But we will still want human educators to make this stuff relatable, and also for the pastoral side of student support. That will remain important.”

fullText:
FARGO, N.D. (AP) — The effort and energy Tim Polasek has poured into North Dakota State's football program on the climb to the FBS can be easily sourced back to his rural roots.

As a small-college quarterback on summer and winter breaks, and later to supplement a meager income as he launched a career in coaching, Polasek worked grueling jobs as a logger in the woods of central Wisconsin and on the overnight shift at a steel mill near his tiny hometown of Iola.

Appreciation for the unglamourous work as a small-college assistant sure comes quick with that background.

"I learned a lot there: That could be you if you don't graduate college and pursue something," said Polasek, who is 28-3 with the Bison since becoming head coach in 2024. "Seeing those tough jobs and other people having to execute that every day really always makes it an honor and a privilege to be the leader of this program."

Having handily beaten Jacksonville State and Fordham in their first two games, the Bison will face one of their biggest tests as a first-year FBS team on Saturday night: Their Mountain West Conference opener at Air Force.

Though five of the strongest programs — Boise State, Colorado State, Fresno State, San Diego State and Utah State — departed this year to restore the Pac-12, the Mountain West restocked with UTEP and North Dakota State and Northern Illinois as football-only members to join holdovers Air Force, Hawaii, Nevada, New Mexico, San Jose State, UNLV and Wyoming.

There's enough relative proximity to the league's geographic footprint and like-minded public institutions for NDSU to see a long-term home that now offers the chance — albeit an annual long shot — to make the College Football Playoff. The Bison won 10 national championships over two decades in the FCS after collecting eight national titles at lower levels.

"We weren't going to go just to go," athletic director Matt Larsen said. "It really had to be the right fit."

Polasek was offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach at Wyoming from 2021-23 under head coach Craig Bohl, his former boss at NDSU. Having spent four seasons as the offensive line coach at Iowa before that, Polasek took the job at Wyoming with an eye toward becoming a head coach himself.

"It was really critical for me to go to Iowa and Wyoming and not be one of the top two or three teams picked in the preseason every year and learn those hard lessons," said Polasek, who turned 47 last month. "There was always chatter that NDSU would fit in the Mountain West."

After becoming the all-time leading passer at Concordia University, an NCAA Division III school near Milwaukee, Polasek spent three years on staff at Wisconsin-Stevens Point. Then he got his first big break with a graduate assistant job under Bohl at North Dakota State, which was two seasons into a jump from Division II to the FCS.

He was put in charge of the running backs a year later, added tight ends to his responsibilities after three more seasons, and returned from a one-year stint at Northern Illinois in 2014 as NDSU's offensive coordinator and running backs coach under head coach Chris Klieman.

Then Polasek got a taste of Big Ten play at Iowa, learning the value of "being brilliant at the basics" under longtime head coach Kirk Ferentz before the jump to Wyoming.

"The second thing I learned from Coach Ferentz is if you treat people right you can cultivate an environment where it's fun to show up to work," Polasek said last month in his office at the Fargodome. "No matter if the portal or NIL and all this stuff exists or not, hey, let's treat each other with respect. Everybody in the building should be able to dance to the music the way they want to dance to it."

The upperclassmen on NDSU's roster were recruited by the previous staff under Matt Entz, who's now the head coach at Fresno State. Polasek's enthusiasm for and experience with the program was immediately palpable to those players.

"He's just hard-nosed and he loves football and he knows the game and he's a people person," said third-year wide receiver and kick returner Jackson Williams. "He's going to take care of us, but at the same time he's going to push us to our limits."

title: Colorado TPUSA chapter enrollment 'flat' after elderly supporter was struck by student with Taco Bell cup
description: Video captured the chaos after Fort Lewis College approved a Turning Point USA chapter, but nearly a year later, membership remains stagnant.
fullText:
Enrollment at the Turning Point USA (TPUSA) chapter at Fort Lewis College in Durango, Colorado, remains flat due to students' fears of retaliation, according to chapter leaders and local supporters. The stagnation comes nearly a year after the campus group's registration sparked intense pushback from the surrounding community and student body.

"It's definitely been flat, I would say," Rachel Cook, vice president of the Fort Lewis College chapter, told Fox News Digital.

Cook's comments come nearly a year after the student government's decision to recognize the chapter touched off severe turmoil on campus — much of which was captured on video and obtained by Fox News Digital.

Erika Kirk Urges Conservative Students Not To Back Down In First School Year Since Charlie's Assassination

One video showed a student being detained by campus police after striking 66-year-old local resident David Peters with a Taco Bell cup outside the student senate chambers.

Peters, former chair of the La Plata County GOP and a retired Chevron executive, reflected on the incident and its lingering effect on the student group.

"Their membership has been essentially flat. The issue is that a lot of students are reluctant to join the chapter for fear of retaliation," Peters said. "And their fears are well-founded. There have been some members who have received anonymous death threats."

Cook echoed those safety concerns.

"One of the main things is that students have said they are hesitant to join because of their personal safety. A lot of our officers have been getting threats and being harassed," she said.

Uc Berkeley Sued For Allegedly Stonewalling Probe Into Violent Ambush At Tpusa Rob Schneider Event

The tensions at Fort Lewis College unfolded amid a national surge in interest for TPUSA campus chapters. Following the September 10, 2025, assassination of TPUSA co-founder Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University, the conservative organization reported receiving more than 120,000 inquiries from students seeking to establish local chapters.

At Fort Lewis College, then-senior Jonah Flynn led the effort to establish a presence on campus. Although the Associated Students of Fort Lewis College (ASFLC) initially rejected Flynn's proposal, the student government ultimately reversed course and voted to approve the group during an emergency session.

The vote prompted immediate outrage from anti-TPUSA spectators waiting outside the meeting room.

According to a Fort Lewis College campus police report, approximately 70 people attended the high-tension meeting. As attendees spilled out into the lobby, an argument broke out between attendees holding opposing views.

The police report states that Peters approached a student who was "booing and yelling" while holding his phone about a foot away to record. The student — identified in police records as Megan Elizabeth Hope Mollett (who goes by Nova and uses they/them pronouns) — struck Peters' phone and hand with an empty Taco Bell cup.

Newly Launched Tpusa Chapter Causes Uproar At Michigan High School Before First Meeting

Officers intervened immediately, separating the pair and detaining Mollett. While the incident was documented as harassment, police released Mollett with a warning after Peters declined to press criminal charges, though he requested that the university take internal disciplinary action.

Reflecting on the fallout nearly a year later, Peters noted that the climate on campus remains hostile.

During the same post-vote protest, David Kozak, a former anthropology professor at the college, was captured on video flipping off the camera and shouting at TPUSA supporters.

"Go on, fascists," Kozak shouted. "Go on, Nazi lovers... C'mon, Nazis!"

A spokesperson for Fort Lewis College confirmed to Fox News Digital that Kozak was retired from the university at the time the incident occurred. "Mr. Kozak retired from Fort Lewis College in 2022 and is no longer employed by the institution," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

The ongoing hostility comes as political violence remains a growing concern across the country following Kirk's assassination. Authorities cited political motivation in the shooting, pointing to evidence including ammunition allegedly engraved with political slogans, highlighting concerns over how inflammatory rhetoric is translating into real-world violence.

Fort Lewis College told Fox News Digital that the institution "takes the safety of our students and visitors seriously. We continue to respond to all reports of safety concerns on campus."

"Fort Lewis College has not received any reports this academic year involving harassment of members of the college's TPUSA chapter. Fort Lewis College has a system in place for students to report negative experiences," a spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

title: New York City pausing some AI tools in schools
description: New York City imposes a one-year moratorium on student-facing AI tools for grades K-8, citing concerns about youth mental health.
fullText:
“A six-year-old child is too young to slice an onion, to fry an egg or to use a stove safely. But once that child becomes 16, that knowledge becomes something they are mature enough to learn,” stressed New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani, while announcing a one-year moratorium on AI tools for students.

In what has been described as one of “the most expansive student-facing AI policies in the country”, the Mayor and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels on September 2 imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for pupils up to eighth grade for the 2026–27 academic year.

Here’s what you need to know about the moratorium, why NYC introduced it, and why the move could set a global precedent.

This move will affect nearly 6,00,000 public school students across the United States’ largest school district. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, while the AI components of more than 38 previously approved programmes that fail to meet the new standards will be disabled or discontinued.

However, not all AI has been banned. Teachers can continue to use approved tools for planning and administrative work. Assistive technologies required by students with disabilities, as well as certain AI tools used in career-readiness programmes, remain permitted where necessary and under the policy’s safeguards.

Five limited AI pilots will also operate throughout the year for high school classrooms. These select tools are Quill (15 minutes per week) for English language arts; Edia (20 minutes per week) for mathematics; Brisk Teaching (10 to 20 minutes once or twice weekly) for teacher-created activities; Playlab (two assignments per marking period; 45 minutes per week) for assignment-specific applications; and Intel AI-Ready Schools (one period per week) to assist students in identifying community issues and developing solutions through term-long projects.

Every high school student will complete two 45-minute modules per year aimed at developing critical thinking around AI use, including its risks, limitations, and scope. Alongside AI restrictions, tighter individual screen-time limits have also been introduced. Children from 2-K through to second grade will have no routine screen time. For those in grades three to five, NYC Public Schools recommends no more than 30 minutes a day of individual screen use; for grades six to eight, the recommendation is 45 minutes. These restrictions do not prohibit teacher-led use of computers, tablets, or interactive whiteboards during lessons.

Throughout the academic year, a panel comprising students, educators, parents, elected officials, union partners, and field experts will assess the impact of the moratorium and pilots, delivering a report with policy recommendations in April 2027.

“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow,” Mr. Mamdani said. “They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators, and wrestle with tough problems on their own.” Mr. Samuels also made a similar argument. Learning, he said, involves getting something wrong, trying again and eventually getting it right. That struggle is not an inconvenience that technology should eliminate; it is part of the learning process.

This move arrives amidst growing concern over screen time harming youth mental health. Studies have linked excessive scrolling, social media exposure and reliance on AI in children to lower critical thinking abilities, shorter attention spans, anxiety, and depression. While evidence connecting AI chatbots to suicide risk remains limited, several cases have prompted lawsuits alleging that interactions with chatbots contributed to young people’s deaths. Mr. Mamdani’s decision follows OpenAI’s launch of a teenage version of ChatGPT on August 18 featuring parental controls and content restrictions regarding self-harm and suicide. On August 26, Meta similarly announced stricter time limits, night-time blocking, and muted notifications during school hours for teenage accounts on Instagram and Facebook.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI-powered early education is not only inevitable but necessary. We do not see it that way,” Mr. Mamdani added.

Research supports a cautious stance. A 2026 CEPR discussion paper by researchers at Stockholm University and the University of Hong Kong examined more than 26,000 students in China over 30 months. They found that access to generative AI increased homework scores by 18% and reduced completion time by 30%. However, after roughly six months, the same students’ closed-book examination scores had fallen by 20%. A broader review by the Brookings Institution’s Centre for Universal Education, analysing over 400 studies and interviews with 500 educators and pupils across 50 countries, concluded that the potential harms of generative AI in primary and secondary education currently outweigh the benefits—though tailored applications with proper safeguards can enrich learning.

How are other parts of the world dealing with a similar dilemma? The United Arab Emirates is moving towards more structured AI education, rather than a moratorium. It has announced an AI curriculum across public and private schools covering areas such as data, algorithms, applications, risks and ethical use. It also plans to train about 22,000 educators in using AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis and lesson planning.

Norway has adopted a more cautious approach. Its education authorities have recommended that pupils in grades one to seven should not be given access to generative AI, while students in eight to 10 should be introduced to it gradually.

Australia has taken another route: a national framework for responsible and ethical use of generative AI in schools, rather than a blanket prohibition. The European Union, meanwhile, has sought to regulate high-risk uses of AI. Under the EU AI Act, certain systems used in education — including those involved in evaluating learning outcomes or determining access to education — can fall into the high-risk category. The legislation does not amount to a general ban on generative AI in schools.

Poland is going further in the opposite direction, investing almost 1.9 billion zloty to equip 12,000 schools with AI laboratory sets as part of its broader digital education push.

And where does India stand? India is closer to the integration camp. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 identifies artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies as important to India’s changing educational and employment landscape, and calls for contemporary subjects such as AI to be introduced at appropriate stages, alongside greater emphasis on computational thinking.

The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) introduced Artificial Intelligence as an optional sixth subject in Class IX from the 2019-20 academic session. More recently, for 2026-27, CBSE launched a dedicated Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence curriculum for Classes III to VIII, with AI and allied-subject curricula for Classes IX to XII also finalised. The curriculum emphasises logical reasoning, pattern recognition, algorithm design, data literacy and responsible and ethical AI use.

fullText:
Student protesters among those hacked, says digital rights group, though Aleksandar Vučić’s government denies spying

At least 14 people from across Serbian civil society were targeted with advanced spyware earlier this year in what the digital rights group Share Foundation said was the largest documented ​wave of such infection in Serbia to date.

The wave of spyware infections was discovered in August after Apple notified people in 110 ⁠countries that they had probably been victims ⁠of mercenary spyware.

The Citizen Lab, which carries out forensic analyses of spyware attacks, released an analysis on Wednesday showing that at least one of the Serbians had been targeted with the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, which would have given the attacker “total access to the device”.

Share said those targeted included members of a Serbian student movement that has been a thorn in the side of the government of Aleksandar Vučić since 2024. Coalescing out of countrywide protests that followed the collapse of a train station that winter, it is one of the largest student movements in Europe.

Vučić has been in power for more than a decade, during which time critics have said he has overseen a hollowing-out of institutions while steering the country closer to Moscow.

There is no evidence that Vučić’s government was the entity that targeted the student with the Pegasus spyware. However, other spyware used against the students, including a software called NoviSpy, has been previously connected to Serbian authorities.

In an interview with Euronews Serbia TV on Wednesday, Ana Brnabić, the parliamentary speaker and a ranking member of the ruling Serbian Progressive party, denied that students had been spied on. “Absolutely not,” she said. “I do not believe a single word they’ve [students, Share] said.”

Share said the timing – during March’s local elections – may have been a practice run before snap elections set for this October.

“This is the largest documented wave of surveillance in Serbia so far,” said Andrijana Ristic, a policy adviser at Share. “We imagine … that the local elections were basically used as a test for the ruling party to see [the spyware’s] strengths, but also to see the amount of pressure they are able to exert over the students and the opposition.”

John Scott-Railton, a senior researcher at the Citizen Lab, said: “Our forensic findings, and this fresh wave of Apple threat notifications reveal that Serbia’s peaceful pro-democracy movement is being aggressively targeted with mercenary spyware ahead of key 2026 election cycles.”

Milica Popović, one of the students who was targeted, called the attacks “cruel”. She said: “Thinking that someone may have entered my private space without my knowledge made me feel so exposed.”

But, she said, the attack, as uncomfortable as it was, would not deter her or the student movement. “If their intention was to frighten us, or make us stop, it will not work.”

NSO Group, which makes Pegasus, a spyware that has been leveraged by authoritarian states to target journalists, human rights campaigners and dissidents, began as an Israeli company with close ties to the military.

It is now under US ownership, and appears to be searching for a way into the US market, including through efforts to get off the US Commerce Department’s blacklist. However, this and other incidents will raise questions about what has been described as their attempt to rebrand as an “ethical spyware company”.

NSO Group has been permanently barred by a US court from targeting WhatsApp users and Meta products. It is unclear if this most recent Pegasus attack happened via WhatsApp.

“Today, Pegasus is still being used to hack people campaigning for democracy. NSO spent a decade promising reform, yet their spyware is still an instrument of political repression,” said Railton.

NSO Group was approached for comment.

fullText:

The victim was identified as Erin Piacenti, 32, of Chester, New Jersey. Piacenti was in her first week back at Bank of America after spending five months caring for her newborn daughter, The New York Times reported.

The NYPD said Piacenti was stabbed near West 42nd Street and Seventh Avenue before being taken to Bellevue Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

Multiple People Stabbed Near Penn Station, Leaving One Seriously Injured As Investigation Continues

Witnesses Recount 'Scary' Nyc Stabbing After Suspect Allegedly Yelled 'Allahu Akbar' During Attacks

"We are shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague," the bank said. "She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed."

title: An Ohio college student died in an apparent suicide. His family says he felt ‘humiliated’ by his ICE ankle monitor
description: Pierre Damas Bel was killed Monday after he stepped into traffic on Interstate 70 near Springfield, Ohio. The Haitian immigrant’s family says he was distraught over being bullied for wearing an ICE an...
fullText:
EDITOR'S NOTE:  This story involves discussion of suicide that some readers may find upsetting. If you feel you are in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the 24-hour Suicide Crisis Lifeline.

Pierre Damas Bel was an avid soccer player at his high school in Springfield, Ohio. He loved being part of JROTC, the US military-sponsored program that provides training to students. And friends and family say he headed to college planning to study neuroscience and excited about the future.

But as the 20-year-old Haitian immigrant began his freshman year at Wright State University, his loved ones say he became increasingly depressed over the ankle monitor he was issued in late July by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The device, they say, sidelined him from playing soccer, stopped him from getting a new ROTC uniform and prompted bullying from some of his classmates.

On Monday morning, the college student made a video call to his father in distress.

"He said, 'Dad, I'm not feeling ok. I'm not thinking right … because of the bullies,' and I told him, 'Come home so that we can talk,'" Pierre Ronal Bel said in a statement.

Soon afterward, the Ohio State Highway Patrol says the 20-year-old got out of his Toyota Avalon on the shoulder of Interstate 70 and stepped into westbound lanes of traffic. The agency says its investigation remains open. Bel's family says they were told he took his own life.

"Police showed up at my door," his father said, "to report that my son had thrown himself under a truck."

Bel was among a growing number of Haitians in Ohio outfitted with the ankle monitors after the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, which allowed them to work legally in the US and protected hundreds of thousands of people across the US from deportation. Immigrant rights advocates are pointing to the young man's apparent suicide as they call for federal officials to stop using the monitors.

"Pierre died as a result of policy. And it's our immigration policy that took his life," Pastor Carl Ruby of the Central Christian Church in Springfield said at a news conference Tuesday, calling on Republican lawmakers to speak out and "put an end to the shackling program before other people end up taking their lives."

Immigration and Customs Enforcement says Bel applied for admission into the United States in Brownsville, Texas, in March 2024 and was released into the country by the Biden administration. The agency issued Bel an ankle monitor on July 29 while he continued his immigration proceedings.

Asked about reports that the student had died by suicide after facing bullying for wearing the device, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement spokesperson said in a written statement that the highway patrol's investigation into the death is ongoing.

"ICE does not comment on the cause of death while that investigation is pending, and we will not speculate about unverified claims regarding other individuals," the spokesperson said, reiterating the administration's push for undocumented immigrants to "self-deport."

"Remaining in the country illegally, while fighting removal, is a choice. Leaving with a free flight home and $2,600 is also a choice," the spokesperson said. "ICE will continue to use detention or alternatives to detention as needed (for) those illegal aliens who stay in violation of the law."

In a statement on its Facebook page, Wright State University did not directly address the bullying allegations, but said counseling and support services had been made available to students, faculty and staff.

"The safety and well-being of our students is the highest priority, and we remain dedicated to providing a campus community where every student feels safe, supported, included and welcomed," the statement said.

Wright State University President Sue Edwards said the school community was heartbroken.

"Pierre was an active honors student who was passionate about soccer and was already actively engaged in his classes and the campus community," she said. "The University mourns the death of Pierre and extends our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones during this unimaginably difficult time."

According to his father, on Friday Bel said something had devastated him in his ROTC class at the school.

"He told me, 'Dad, I felt humiliated … Everyone got uniforms, except for me, because of the bracelet," Pierre Ronal Bel said.

Wright State said questions about the ROTC program and its participation requirements and uniform issuance should be directed to the United States Army Cadet Command.

A spokesperson for the US Army Cadet Command told CNN the ankle monitor wasn't the reason Bel did not receive a uniform. Bel was not eligible to become a cadet in the ROTC program because of his immigration status, the spokesperson said, and therefore was taking the class as an elective and could not be issued a uniform. Class leadership was "very supportive" of him joining the class, the spokesperson said.

In recent social media posts, Bel described the ankle monitor and how difficult it was for him to wear it.

"I came to this country to pursue my education. I didn't come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone. Yet now I'm walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience," he wrote in a July 30 Instagram post, which included a series of pictures of him at awards and recognition ceremonies.

"I came here to study, to build my future, and to live a better (life) not to be treated like criminal. So now, how am I supposed play college sports with a GPS monitor on my leg?"

The student also shared testimonials from Springfield High School teachers and coworkers at a Texas Roadhouse restaurant, apparently provided as letters of support in his pending immigration case, praising his work ethic and leadership skills.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican who's been a vocal critic of the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for Haitians, told reporters Tuesday that Bel's death was a "horrible tragedy." And at a news conference Tuesday in Springfield, community leaders and immigrant rights advocates slammed the way they said authorities had treated Bel and other Haitians, many of whom have been living in fear since their deportation protections were revoked.

The ankle monitors are part of a frequently used ICE program known as "alternatives to detention." But advocates say that for many Haitians in Springfield, the devices evoke the painful history of shackles worn during slavery. The day before Bel's death, demonstrators marched in a protest dubbed "Unshackle Springfield."

Advocates estimate that ankle monitors have been issued to hundreds of Haitians in Springfield in the past month, and many in the Columbus area as well.

"There's nothing illegal or criminalizing about Pierre Damas Bel, not even a traffic ticket, and it shouldn't have to get to this point for this administration to understand that there's blood on their hands," said Yola Lamarre of the Haitian Community Network. "There's nothing just about shackling people that have not ever committed a crime. … This was a situation that could have been prevented."

Lamarre, who organizers described as a close friend and mentor to Bel, said she'd spoken with him multiple times about his concerns over the ankle monitor.

"Pierre shared a lot of depressive thoughts with me after we saw the ankle monitor situation being targeted to Haitians in Springfield," she said, tearing up as she described her friend to reporters. "Pierre Damas Bel was not a criminal, but he was treated as one."

CNN's Omar Jimenez and Lizzie Jury contributed to this report.

fullText:
Teachers and parents have warned against AI use in schools over concerns of ‘cognitive surrender’

New York City will ban students’ use of artificial intelligence in public schools through eighth grade, typically age 13 or 14. The prohibition is scheduled to be announced on Wednesday and will go into effect next week.

The change is part of a sweeping overhaul of the use of technology in the US’s largest school district, which enrolls roughly 900,000 students a year. In another policy shift, classrooms will keep students off laptops or tablets through the third grade, age nine or 10. The city’s public school technology policies are closely watched by the rest of the United States.

Teachers and parents have warned against the use of AI instructional software in schools over concerns about harming children’s mental health and cognitive development, in particular an abdication of reasoning to software, a phenomenon researchers have dubbed “cognitive surrender”, as well as environmental damage.

AI use will only be allowed in high school, which begins in the ninth grade in the US school system. Even then, it will be limited to specific uses, such as learning about the technology itself.

AI “companion chatbots” offering psychological support will also be banned. The rules allow teachers to use AI for tasks including preparing lessons or writing messages, but they are forbidden from asking AI to grade assignments.

The city’s education department recommends limiting screen time to 45 minutes in class for middle schoolers – sixth through eighth grade – and 30 minutes for elementary school students. But the question remains of how to monitor AI use, since it often takes place outside the school environment.

The new rules follow an initial framework published in March, which used a traffic light system to determine which tasks AI would be used for. In 2023, the school system forbade students’ use of ChatGPT, though the ban was reversed less than a year later.

The 2026 framework, which allowed students to use AI for research, exploration and creative projects, sparked fury among many parents and teachers who considered it too lenient.

In response, the city’s schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels, said that leaders had “missed the mark” in their communications, adding his office would carefully review parents’ feedback for incorporation into future rules.

The city had long planned to follow the March framework with a more comprehensive “guidebook” to take feedback into account, the education department has said.

The department will set up a taskforce made up of teachers, elected officials, experts and union representatives. The taskforce is to produce a report in April, intended to serve as the basis for New York’s AI-in-schools policy.

title: Pennsylvania police officer charged with voluntary manslaughter in killing of college student
description: Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin Steele said Upper Pottsgrove Police Cpl.  Sean Farrell, 58, is charged in the Aug. 23 death of Glenwood Earl Pysher IV.  The prosecutor said the officer had l...
fullText:
NORRISTOWN, Pa. (AP) — A Pennsylvania police officer who fatally shot a 22-year-old college student, who had ended up at the wrong house late at night and was waiting for friends to pick him up, has been charged with voluntary manslaughter, a prosecutor said Tuesday.

Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin Steele said Upper Pottsgrove Police Cpl. Sean Farrell, 58, is charged in the Aug. 23 death of Glenwood Earl Pysher IV. The prosecutor said the officer had less-than-lethal options and did not need to resort to shooting Pysher during the encounter.

The Montgomery County Detective Bureau investigated the shooting and reviewed footage from Farrell's body-worn camera, the district attorney's office said in a news release.

"The investigation found that Cpl. Farrell had less-than-lethal options on his utility belt that he did not employ, including a taser. At the time of the shooting, the officer was a safe distance from Pysher behind a car, and the victim had his hands in the air and did not possess any type of weapon. Mr. Pysher was not a threat. This is not a legal use of deadly force, leading to the charge of Voluntary Manslaughter," Steele said in a news release.

An attorney for Pysher's family issued a statement thanking the prosecutor.

"The family is grateful for the work of the Montgomery County District Attorney's office and they are looking forward to justice in this horribly tragic, preventable and reckless conduct that took the life of their son," said attorney Ken Fulginiti.

Farrell turned himself in to the Montgomery County Detectives on Tuesday. Magisterial District Judge Kathleen Rebar set bail at $75,000, and Farrell must turn in all weapons to the state police as a condition of his release, a spokesperson for the district attorney's office said. He has a preliminary hearing set for Sept. 10.

Farrell was the first officer on the scene after a resident called 911 to report someone trying to break into the back door of a home. Farrell's body-worn camera showed the officer walking down the driveway with his gun drawn, using its light to illuminate the way, the release says.

Standing behind a car in the driveway, Farrell saw Pysher on the home's patio, near the back door. Farrell yelled, "Police, let me see your hands." Then he yelled, "Hands up, hands up now, drop to the ground."

Pysher is seen on video raising his hands as he began walking toward the officer and continuing to walk in that direction as the officer yelled, "Drop to the ground," the release said. Farrell again yelled, "Drop to the ground," then yelled, "Stop or I'll..." But before he finished the sentence, Farrell fired two shots, hitting Pysher twice in the chest, the district attorney's office said.

Pysher was 17 to 20 feet (5 to 6 meters) from the officer when he was shot, the release says.

The investigation found that Pysher had been out at several bars earlier in the evening to celebrate a friend's 21st birthday. A designated driver drove the group to the home of the person whose birthday it was around 11 p.m., and Pysher left about half an hour later to walk half a mile to another friend's house to keep drinking but ended up at the wrong house, the release says.

Pysher's father has said he believes, based on what his son's friends have told him, that his son tried to enter what he thought was his friend's house.

"He tried to open the doorknob and obviously startled the homeowner," Glen Pysher told The Associated Press last week. "From what we understand, he announced, 'Hey! Open the door!' because he thought he was at his friend's house."

His son then sat down on the back porch and contacted his friends, who realized he was in the wrong place and set out to find him, the father said.

Brumback reported from Atlanta.

title: Gen Z Democratic lawmaker spars with Baby Boomers over whether American Dream is dead
description: Democratic Rep. Maxwell Frost clashed with Baby Boomers over student debt, housing prices, and whether the American dream still exists today.
fullText:
Rep. Maxwell Frost, D-Fla., engaged in a fiery debate with a group of Baby Boomers this week on the web series Surrounded, arguing that Generation Z faces economic hurdles their generation did not experience.

The 29-year-old congressman appeared in the viral debate on the Jubilee YouTube channel, where a single public figure faces an entire room of challengers.

In the debate, Frost argued that young Americans were raised with the expectation that going to college — even if it required taking on student debt — would lead to a good job, allow them to repay that debt and provide a pathway toward the American dream. He argued that this bargain, and the American dream prospect itself, no longer holds for many young Americans.

Frost cited his working-class family background and noted that he worked as an Uber driver to make ends meet while running for Congress.

Vance Warns There Will Be A Socialist President In This Country If Gop Doesn't Fix Economy For Young People

"So that's the American dream! You lived it!" his debate opponent, comedian Geno Bisconte, responded in a clip that went viral on Monday.

"The American dream isn't driving Uber to barely make ends meet," Frost replied. "The American dream is upward mobility and being able to have success."

"You went from driving an Uber to being a politician!" Bisconte shouted. "Is that upward!? What am I missing?"

"But it's not about one person. It's about the totality of a generation," Frost replied. "That's part of the reason that I have the claim that I have. The majority of my generation is struggling and having a hard time to just survive. Just to survive. The American dream isn't survival, my friend. Is the American dream survival or is it thriving? The American dream is thriving. The fact of the matter is the vast majority of young people feel like they're not able to put aside enough money to have mobility."

Another participant named William argued that many of Frost's complaints can be attributed to population growth from mass immigration.

Biden's Illegal Immigration Surge Caused Higher Rent And Home Prices, Fed Study Finds

"When we started school, there was less than 157 million people in America today. Now there's 340," William responded. "More people needing homes means home prices go up. More people needing food means food prices go up. We can't correct that until we get rid of all the foreigners that have come in here. And your party is refusing to do that, even if they're illegal!"

Frost pushed back, saying immigrants provide a net economic positive and share 

He added that entry-level wages haven't kept pace with living costs, making the prospect of buying a home on a retail or service job "a fantasy." Frost also pointed to competition in real estate, noting young buyers now face off against private equity firms.

Analysts and policy experts offered mixed takes on the generational exchange in comments to Fox News Digital.

Judge Glock, director of research and a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, argued that in general young adults have a much higher net income than Baby Boomers did at the same age, but agreed that housing affordability is at its "worst it's been in decades." However, Glock disputed Frost's contention that institutional investors or older generations are to blame, attributing price spikes to regulatory constraints that limit new housing construction alongside high mortgage rates.

Ceo Under Fire For Mass Layoffs Amid Foreign Worker Hiring Spree Now Appointed To Fed's Task Force On Jobs

"Frost is wrong that higher housing prices are due to competition from Baby Boomers or Wall Street," Glock said. "The fundamental reason housing prices have gone up is that we are building less than we used to. And we are building less than we used to because of ever-increasing regulations, from zoning to environmental mandates. When combined with high mortgage rates due to both inflation and high levels of government debt, homeownership is becoming increasingly out of reach."

Glock also noted that "This generation also has much higher student debt levels than earlier ones. Due to their high student debt, and lack of wealth in housing, older Millennials have a lower net worth than Gen Xers at the same age. That's not because of a lack of jobs, but because colleges have been handing out ever more low-quality degrees at an ever higher cost."

Elizabeth Pipko, a former Republican National Committee national spokesperson, agreed that Gen Z faces certain major challenges, but argued they should not overestimate the luxuries the Baby Boomer generation had.

"Nobody is arguing that young Americans have it easy. And it is true that housing prices in many parts of America have risen much faster than incomes, particularly in desirable cities and suburbs. But, with that being said, times have changed and the comparison to baby boomers is not exactly fair," she said. "Households back then consumed much less. Today's family is purchasing a much higher material standard of living. What is considered 'normal' today would have been a dream to many a few decades ago. For example, the material things that improve our quality of life which were mere dreams are now not only attainable by most, but vastly cheaper. Think about computers, televisions, household technology, air travel, etc. Times have changed, yes, and with that comes difficulties, but also incredible advantages and benefits."

Click Here For More Coverage Of Media And Culture

Pipko added that immigration, artificial intelligence, and post-pandemic work shifts are compounding the tough entry-level job market for recent graduates. She cautioned against abusing H-1B visas for cheaper labor, warning that such practices put "American graduates in direct competition for the entry-level jobs that traditionally gave them their start."

Link Lauren, an influencer and former senior advisor to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., also told Fox News Digital, "For years, I've recommended trade and technical schools. If you go to college and major in queer theater or LatinX literature, don't be shocked when there aren't tons of jobs waiting for you. Unless you really need that four-year degree to go on to medical school or law school, you really have to think twice about spending all that time and money on a college campus. The American dream is certainly attainable. But the landscape has shifted. This is something Charlie Kirk spoke about often."

Fox News Digital also reached out to Frost's campaign and did not receive an immediate reply.

fullText:
Everton have agreed a £40m deal to sign USA international Folarin Balogun from Monaco, with a medical set to take place on Tuesday.

So what type of player will the Blues be signing and how does he compare with Thierno Barry, the Toffees' current first-choice striker?

A one-time Arsenal academy graduate, Balogun joined Monaco from the Gunners for £35m in 2023, going on to score 31 goals in 91 appearances for the Ligue 1 club.

He missed four months of the 2024-25 campaign due to injury but after returning to fitness in April he enjoyed the most prolific season of his career to date in 2025-26, scoring 19 goals in 43 games, including five in the Champions League.

Whereas Barry is more of a target man adept at winning balls in the air, Balogun boasts greater pace and a game built around making runs behind opposition defences.

At the World Cup earlier this summer, the 25-year-old averaged eight runs in behind per game, ranking him third of all strikers, and scored three goals.

His goals-per-minute ratio was almost identical to that of Beto, who is leaving Everton for Fiorentina in a £15m deal, in league football last season.

But Balogun's younger age and Champions League experience suggest his ceiling could be comparatively higher.

His tally of 19 goals last season is at least seven more than either Beto or Barry have managed in a campaign with a club in an elite European league.

title: Dad of third-grade girl in Massachusetts allegedly barged in on by trans student in bathroom calls for action
description: Massachusetts father of third grader alleges transgender student barged in girls stalls and is taking complaint to federal level.
fullText:
The Massachusetts father of a third-grade girl who says his daughter was subjected to a disturbing bathroom incident involving a transgender classmate is not backing down from his fight with the school district.

Luis Rivera, whose daughter attends Rochester Memorial School, has hired attorney Sam Whiting of the Massachusetts Liberty Legal Center after filing a federal Title IX complaint against the Old Rochester Regional School District in May.

A letter filed by Whiting on Rivera's behalf alleges that Rivera's 9-year-old daughter was the victim of sex-based harassment after a transgender female classmate, who was born male, entered her bathroom stall. The letter also alleges that the student had previously watched female students use the bathroom, which Rivera and his attorney argue invaded their privacy and undermined their dignity.

Rivera and his wife, Kerri, along with other parents, have repeatedly contacted Rochester Memorial School Principal Heidi Letendre about the transgender student's use of the girls' bathroom, according to the letter.

Washington Mother Says She Found Adult Male Showering In Women's Locker Room During Children's Swim Meet

"On numerous occasions, during this actual event, we reached out multiple times. And we were told by the principal that no boy is supposed to be in the bathroom. Then somewhere along the line, they changed their story," Rivera told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital reached out to Letendre for comment.

Rivera said he has attended every school committee meeting since the incident, joining other community members in pushing the district to change its bathroom policy.

He also said he and his wife have decided to remove their daughter from the school for the upcoming school year. His daughter wrote a letter to President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump asking for help with the situation.

"I feel scared to use the girls' bathroom," she wrote.

Washington Mother Pulls Children From School After Pride Lesson Shown In Music Class Without Notice

The dispute centers not only on the alleged incident involving Rivera's daughter but also on the district's interpretation of state and federal anti-discrimination laws, Whiting said.

Massachusetts law prohibits discrimination against students based on protected characteristics, including gender identity, and bars schools from excluding students from "the advantages, privileges and courses of study" they offer.

The Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education also says transgender students should have access to school facilities, including bathrooms, consistent with their gender identity.

For now, however, the Old Rochester Regional School District does not appear to have plans to change its policy regarding transgender students.

In a message to parents, Superintendent Michael Nelson said that, following a Title IX investigation, school staff and district administrators acted in compliance with the law. The decision, he said, was made by an independent decision maker following the complaint brought forward by the Rochester Memorial School parent.

Trump Admin Targets Woke Schools Accused Of Hiding Students' Gender Transitions From Parents

In a written statement, Nelson said the district is bound by the Massachusetts laws.

"Additionally, our schools adhere to the policies and procedures of the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education," he said.

"... We believe that we are bound by law and state education policy and that age-appropriate handling of student matters in a public school setting is best left to the professional educators who know how to do their jobs correctly and effectively," he said.

He also noted that during this process, his educators and administrators have been subject to "innumerable explicit, angry and threatening communications," directly and indirectly through social media.

Fox News Digital reached out directly to Nelson.

Whiting said he and the parents involved are particularly disappointed by the superintendent's response, which he claims downplayed the seriousness of the incident.

According to Whiting, the response amounted to, "Oh, these things just happen between 9-year-olds… sometimes bathroom doors are unlocked and these things happen."

Portland Parent Banned From School Events After Opposing Gender Identity Assignment Files Lawsuit

Whiting said he hopes the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights will investigate the complaint.

"Ultimately, we hope they will find that the school district is in violation of Title IX and will refer the case to the Department of Justice for enforcement," he said. "School districts who violate Title IX can be at risk of losing their federal funds… We're always hopeful they'll do the right thing, but if they don't, our plan is to try to get this in front of the proper authorities at the federal level."

Rivera said the lack of what he considers meaningful action from the district has left him with no choice but to escalate the matter.

"They haven't taken any remedial action. And so that's why we feel like we have to kind of bring this up to the higher authorities and the federal government," Rivera said. "There's no transparency. There's no accountability. It's just they're running around free, and they're violating these girls' privacy rights, because what happened to my daughter should have never happened if the policies were put into place."

"And I have to deal with her emotional trauma behind this," Rivera added.

title: Decontamination ongoing after MIT student reports creating dimethyl mercury
description: The school said the graduate student showed no signs of mercury exposure in an initial blood test but was under medical supervision as of Aug. 29.
fullText:
A Massachusetts Institute of Technology building was expected to remain closed at least through Aug. 30 after a graduate student was said to have created an unauthorized, highly toxic chemical compound.

The school's Aug. 29 statement said the student, who was not publicly identified, self-reported to an emergency room and said they had synthesized dimethyl mercury on Aug. 26. Less than 0.1 milliliters of the compound is a "severely toxic dose," according to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.

Dartmouth College professor Karen Wetterhahn died in 1997 after spilling "a few drops" of dimethyl mercury on her glove, according to the New Hampshire school. She developed health problems months after the spill that were discovered to be effects of acute mercury poisoning.

The MIT student showed no sign of mercury exposure in an initial blood test, the school said. The Aug. 29 statement also said updated information "calls into question" whether dimethyl mercury was synthesized.

The school said the student was under medical supervision and that Building 18 remained closed as "specialized decontamination efforts continue out of an abundance of caution."

High-touch surfaces in common areas of the student's residence hall were professionally cleaned, and decontamination of their individual unit was ongoing, MIT said. No restrictions were placed on the building.

Individuals who were near the student and affected workspace on Aug. 26 were offered baseline testing. Officials believe there is "very low risk of secondary or tertiary exposures" and do not recommend testing for individuals who were not in the student's lab space that day, the school said.

BrieAnna Frank is a First Amendment reporter at USA TODAY. Reach her at bjfrank@usatoday.com.

title: Hong Kong's independent bookstores, a refuge for Chinese readers, are under threat
description: Chinese university student Fleming Cheng found the political books he had only glimpsed online in a Hong Kong bookstore last year.  Before visiting Greenfield Book Store, Cheng had only managed to see...
fullText:
HONG KONG (AP) — Chinese university student Fleming Cheng found the political books he had only glimpsed online in a Hong Kong bookstore last year.

Before visiting Greenfield Book Store, Cheng had only managed to see the books' covers online after bypassing Beijing's internet censorship using a VPN. At the store, he picked up a title offering a critical account of China. He stood there devouring dozens of pages from another, about a pro-reform Chinese leader who fell from power for sympathizing with the protesters during the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy movement in 1989.

Cheng said he saw perspectives diverging from the mainland's official narrative.

Hong Kong's independent bookstores, many of them tucked away from busy streets inside buildings, have long offered a refuge and a window to a freer world for some mainland Chinese readers seeking ideas suppressed at home.

But these spaces now are under threat following a wave of bookseller arrests over alleged sedition under a 2024 national security law. Critics say their plight reflected the city's broader crackdown on dissent that began after Beijing imposed a separate 2020 security law. Authorities say the two laws are vital to stability.

Greenfield was one of four bookstores targeted by police in just four months. Although bail was granted, the 50-year-old shop in July announced it would close at the end of its lease. Another bookstore, Have A Nice Stay, set up by former journalists, had announced plans to shut down Sunday, citing "elusive red lines" and financial challenges, even before its booksellers were arrested on the same day as Greenfield's.

"If the Hong Kong government desperately tries to bring every aspect of the city into close alignment with the mainland, or even to the point where the two become indistinguishable, that would be a tremendous loss for us mainlanders too," Cheng said.

Hong Kong, a former British colony that returned to China in 1997, was once known for its freedoms of publication and expression.

But in 2015, bookseller Lam Wing-kee and four others affiliated with Causeway Bay Books disappeared. The store was known for selling politically sensitive titles. Lam later told reporters he was held by Chinese authorities, providing explosive details that contradicted official Chinese accounts. Gossipy books about Chinese politics soon dwindled on Hong Kong's shelves.

After the 2020 security law, leading activists were arrested and civil society groups disbanded. Titles about the Tiananmen crackdown and works by pro-democracy politicians were pulled from public libraries. At the city's annual book fair, some smaller book businesses were barred from exhibiting, and a pro-Beijing newspaper labeled an independent book fair a form of "soft resistance."

Despite the pressure and increased official inspections, many pressed on, with some continuing to organize activities alongside selling books.

But the arrests hit Book Punch in March, Hunter Bookstore in June, and Greenfield and Have A Nice Stay in July. The authorities accused the booksellers of selling seditious publications, according to government statements and media reports.

Authorities say statements with "seditious intention" to incite hatred against or the overthrow of the governments of China and Hong Kong are prohibited. But they have not specified the books they consider as "seditious," leaving observers to find clues in news reports quoting anonymous sources.

Secretary for Security Chris Tang said the law is clear about what constitutes seditious intent and reiterated there would be no banned book list. He said booksellers should ensure the titles they sell do not harm national security, just as those selling food need to ensure the food won't cause a stomach ache or be poisonous.

A bookseller, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of government retribution, said they struggled to judge what was seditious. Still, they became more cautious about whether to sell certain books on China's modern politics. Their landlord was also reviewing whether to continue to rent the space to them after being harassed.

In an emailed reply, the government condemned any "smearing" and false remarks regarding the work in safeguarding national security. It said the security laws clearly stipulate that human rights, freedoms of speech and publication should be protected.

The offenses linked to seditious intention expressly protect expression of opinions or even criticism against government policies, it said.

University student Iris Wang from neighboring Guangdong sensed tighter control over Hong Kong. To her, Hunter encouraged people to think, instead of just selling books like its mainland peers. She bought a postcard about being courageous and a manga there.

Some mainland readers also visit the stores for non-political reasons, such as for their niche books or simply for their calmness.

Hong Konger Brian Leung found companionship in independent bookstores, saying each had its own character. When arrests happened at the shops he visited, he said he felt something he cherished and that Hong Kong deserved was being rejected.

"Part of what I have grown used to in Hong Kong is lost again," he said, adding that the bookshops have not "incited" him because readers can judge for themselves.

In Taiwan, widely seen as the freest publishing hub for Chinese-language books, some publishers have filled the gap as restrictions deepened in Hong Kong after the 2020 security law took effect. Some readers fear one day Taiwan cannot send books to Hong Kong as freely as before.

Taiwan's publishers released six times as many books about Hong Kong between 2020 and 2024 as in the previous five years, according to Cheng Tsu-Bang, a sociology professor at Tunghai University in Taiwan.

"The publication of books seems to have become a very important medium of communication between Taiwan and Hong Kong, or a medium of mutual support," he said.

In July, Taiwan's broadcaster FTV reported that a logistics firm stopped taking orders to ship books from Taiwan to Hong Kong bookstores under investigation. It also demanded a full book list before delivering to other Hong Kong premises, the report added.

One Hong Kong author who moved to Taiwan and has published books there is Lee, who spoke on condition of not using their full name out of fear of government retribution.

Lee has written about Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement, saying the independent bookstores served as a bridge to bring works about Hong Kong to the city and connect diaspora writers to their home.

The writer compared the collapse of civil society to a boulder rolling downhill, crushing things in its path. Lee said bookstores were a small flower field where people could breathe and try to safeguard what remained.

"It's now like being told very directly and cruelly that perhaps this borrowed time is coming to an end," Lee said.

title: Star student rejected by 16 colleges, hired by Google, gets legal win in racial discrimination suit
description: A Palo Alto, California, father declares victory after a judge denied the University of Washington's motion to dismiss their anti-Asian bias suit.
fullText:
A father in Palo Alto, California is declaring a victory in court after a federal judge allowed a civil rights lawsuit alleging anti-Asian bias in college admissions to move forward.

Nan Zhong and his son, Stanley Zhong, filed federal lawsuits against several elite institutions — including the University of California system, the University of Washington, the University of Michigan, and Cornell University. The complaints allege the universities engaged in "racially discriminatory admissions practices that disadvantage highly qualified Asian-American applicants."

One of their cases will now proceed in part against the University of Washington after a federal judge granted the university defendants' motion to dismiss in part and denied it in part.

"We got an exciting ruling from the judge," Nan Zhong told Fox News Digital. "Effectively, the judge ruled in our favor by denying the university's motion to dismiss. So this is a major development in the lawsuit. That means the judge found enough factual allegations to support our allegation."

Duke Law's Alleged Race-based Admissions Accused Of Defying Supreme Court Ruling: Doj

The ruling centered in part on sovereign immunity. Judge James L. Robart denied the defendants' motion to dismiss Stanley's Title VI claims against the university while dismissing several other claims.

The University of Washington Board of Regents sent Fox News Digital a statement in response to the ruling.

"We're pleased that the court dismissed many of the claims and two of the three plaintiffs. Admission to the Allen School is highly competitive and the vast majority of out-of-state applicants are not admitted because, as Washington's flagship university, we prioritize Washington residents for admission," a spokesperson said.

"With that ruling, we can now proceed into discovery, request internal documents, internal communication, and most importantly, admissions data," Nan said.

Stanley Zhong, now 21, made headlines after he was rejected by 16 of the 18 colleges he applied to — including top-tier public and private institutions — despite boasting an elite academic record. A 2023 graduate of Gunn High School in Palo Alto, Stanley scored a 1590 out of 1600 on the SAT (99th percentile), held a 4.42 weighted GPA, ranked in the top 9% of his graduating class, and had launched a free e-signing startup featured by Amazon Web Services.

Shortly after the college rejections, Google hired Stanley as a full-time software engineer in a position that his family's court filing says typically requires a Ph.D. or equivalent practical experience. Stanley was first scouted by the tech giant in coding competitions when he was just 13 years old.

California Sociology Professor Cited 'Irony' In Removing Act/sat, Not Fixing Racial Disparities As Intended

The family spent over a year researching admissions trends before filing the lawsuits, concluding that anti-Asian bias remains a systemic issue despite recent court precedents.

"The story is much bigger than myself, than my son, Stanley, or our family," Zhong told Fox News Digital. "First of all, I have a younger son, so I don't want him to face the same problem that his older brother faced. I think this is something important we should correct so my future grandkids won't have the same problem again."

Zhong added that since taking their battle public, dozens of families across the country have reached out to share similar experiences.

"After the story came out, we received a lot of communication from other Asian-American families telling us about their story, telling about how highly qualified Asian-American students were rejected left and right," Zhong said. "So this is a large-scale issue and I think of it as an issue that's been around for a long time."

California Board Of Regents To Review Sat/act Testing Ban After 1,400 Professors Warn Of 'Severe' Math Gaps

Spokespersons for the University of California system have previously denied the allegations, maintaining that their admissions policies strictly comply with state and federal laws prohibiting race-conscious decisions.

Stanley Zhong was accepted at the University of Maryland and the University of Texas-Austin but decided to take a job offer as a software development engineer at Google in the fall of 2023 instead.

title: Former Texas high school teacher arrested after probe into inappropriate student relationship
description: Holly Adams, an Angleton High School teacher, faces charges of tampering with evidence and furnishing alcohol to minors after a year-long investigation.
fullText:
A former Texas schoolteacher was arrested Tuesday amid allegations of inappropriate relationships with students, nearly one year after authorities began investigating her.

Holly Adams, who taught at Angleton High School near Houston, is charged with one count of tampering with evidence and two counts of purchasing or furnishing alcohol to a minor, the Brazoria County Sheriff's Office said.

The probe began after a student told school staff that Adams was having an inappropriate relationship with a former student, KTRK-TV reported.

Texas Substitute Teacher Accused Of Improper Relationship With Student, Alarming Parents

The student told school officials that the victim FaceTime-called him over the summer from a bedroom in Adams' house and that the bed was covered in nude photos of her, according to the news outlet. Another image depicted Adams and the former student cuddling, the report states.

Adams reportedly invited students to her home to perform chores, and she allegedly admitted to speaking with three members of the school baseball team on Snapchat.

High School Teacher Who Allegedly Had Sex With Student In Closet Now Faces Charges Involving More Teens

Many female teachers who sexually abuse male students sometimes convice themselves that the relationship is legitimate, said Gail Saltz, MD, Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry at Weill Cornell Medical College.

"They're more likely to be psychologically both grooming their victim, but also what's called self grooming," Saltz told Fox News Digital. "They are convincing themselves that what they are doing is having an intimate, romantic relationship that is benefiting the victim as well."

Saltz noted that the damage done to the male students is just as damaging as female victims.

"It is easily as damaging in terms of, you've been abused by an adult. And that adult took advantage of your trust," she said. "That violated boundaries that you weren't ready for."

Adams was taken to the Brazoria County Detention Center and released on a $26,000 bond the same day. She no longer works for the Angleton Independent School District, a spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the sheriff's office.

title: Florida Students Punished for Silent Protest Against ICE Get Free Speech Victory in Federal Court
description: A federal judge sided with the Florida International University students who sued over their school's student expression policy.
fullText:
A group of Florida students returning to college may have scored a temporary free speech win, but their legal battle may not be over.

On Sunday, a federal judge ruled that Florida International University (FIU) likely violated students' free speech rights when the school punished students for silently protesting indoors, reported Axios. In her ruling, U.S. Southern District of Florida Judge Jacqueline Becerra issued a preliminary injunction, preventing the school from enforcing its expressive activity rule against the students.

The case stems from an incident in March when a group of students wearing shirts saying "ICE OFF FIU" stood in silence for "a few minutes" while the school's president hosted a talk with former MLB player Alex Rodriguez on campus, reported WLRN. The students were protesting the "school's voluntary collaboration with immigration enforcement on campus," the outlet reported. 

FIU charged seven of the students who participated with misconduct, and six received written reprimands. The school also ordered the students to record two-minute "video reflections" explaining their understanding of the school's expressive activities policy and how they will "apply" what they "learned moving forward."

The disciplinary action drew the attention of civil liberties organizations, including the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE). On June 18, the group sent a letter to FIU urging the school "to drop the conduct charges and revise its expressive activities policy to protect such expression inside university facilities."

The school did not take action. On August 11, the punished students sued the school and members of its administration. In addition to requesting compensatory damages, the suit argued that FIU's Regulation 110(3)—which prohibits "protests, parades, marches, picketing, demonstrations, and other similar expressive activities" inside university buildings—"blatantly violate[d] the Plaintiffs' First Amendment rights" and should be declared unconstitutional. The rule also states that "university indoor facilities are designed for instruction, study, reflection, group discussion, research, administrative functions, and other University activities and operations," and "this provision will be enforced in a content and viewpoint neutral manner."

Becerra, citing the Vietnam War-era free speech case Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District, found that the plaintiffs were "substantially likely to prevail" in their challenge against FIU's unconstitutional policy. The ruling also notes that "based on the evidence submitted to date, it does not appear that any Plaintiff, or anyone else wearing an 'ICE OFF FIU' T-shirt, spoke or did anything other than sit, stand, and walk."

According to Inside Higher Ed, university officials have "previously maintained that the policy is compliant with the First Amendment and Florida laws." It's unclear whether FIU will appeal. A school representative told Axios that the university would "comply with the court's order while considering our legal options." 

Regardless of whether one agrees with the students' message, FIU's punishment of the silent protesters should concern free speech defenders. Perhaps the most disturbing part of FIU's punishment was forcing students to record video apologies for silently and non-disruptively expressing their views. Bret Weinstein, a longtime opponent of campus cancel culture, weighed in on the situation, writing on X, "Commitment to freedom of speech requires us to oppose compelled speech every bit as strongly as we oppose censorship." Hopefully, by this school year, other universities will adopt this principled stance.
